chosen.title: The Algorithm Did It Is Not a Defense: How the Courts Ended AI's Accountability Holiday
chosen.rationale: As of mid-2026 a wave of rulings (Garcia v. Character Technologies, the pending OpenAI wrongful-death and school-shooting suits) has rejected Section 230 and First Amendment shields and let product-liability and failure-to-warn claims proceed against AI makers — the first time the 'someone has to answer' question is being decided in court, not a press release. This is Dawn's exact terrain: who is finally held liable when a machine harms, and who spent years engineering the shield that said no one was.

rejected_candidates.title: Reading the Worker: The Fight to Keep AI Out of Your Emotions and Your Brain
rejected_candidates.rationale: California's AB 1883 — banning employers from using AI to infer workers' emotional states or collect 'neural data' — cleared the legislature August 30, 2026 and sits on Newsom's desk with a September 30 deadline, making emotion-and-brain surveillance the live labor-rights flashpoint right now. It's a fresh angle distinct from AIMA's keystroke-surveillance and algorithmic-boss pieces: the frontier has moved from what you type to what you feel and what your nervous system does — precisely Dawn's surveillance-meets-labor-meets-bodily-autonomy beat.

rejected_candidates.title: The Bias-Audit Industrial Complex: Who Watches the Algorithm, and Who Pays Them
rejected_candidates.rationale: 2026's defining regulatory shift is the move from companies grading their own homework to mandatory independent third-party bias audits (Colorado SB 24-205's June 30 deadline, NYC/Illinois/NY layered audit rules, EEOC's 'the algorithm did it is no defense' stance) — spawning a fast-growing compliance-audit industry. Dawn's 'follow the money' instinct fits: an audit paid for by the audited is a new form of accountability theater, and someone is quietly building a market on it.
